source.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?

page_placements.theme: Developmental order: induction heads relative to other circuits and abilities

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document problem; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction behavior and compares the causal effects of induction and function-vector heads on few-shot accuracy and token-loss difference. Its results qualify the claim that induction heads are the main driver of ICL, especially by separating these two measures.
record.gate_note: The study reports head-score measurements, head ablations, and training trajectories that bear on the claim. Detailed task-by-task and model-by-model plots are not transcribed as separate numeric rows where the text gives only aggregate conclusions; those plots do not provide extractable numeric values in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: Ablations across 12 pretrained LMs (70M–7B) compare induction and FV heads on few-shot accuracy and on Olsson et al.'s token-loss difference. Pythia checkpoints track induction-score emergence against ICL accuracy. The authors argue the 'induction heads drive ICL' view needs restating.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that FV heads, not induction heads, mainly drive few-shot ICL accuracy, increasingly so with scale. They attribute earlier claims to using token-loss difference, on which induction heads matter more, and to not controlling for induction–FV head overlap. They speculate that induction heads are precursors that many FV heads evolve from. They also say the scale dependence challenges strong universality.
record.recipe_differences: Measures induction scores on synthetic repeated-token sequences and identifies FV heads using causal mediation; compares mean-ablation effects on task accuracy and token-loss difference. It is not a reproduction of the original small attention-only training experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative effects differ by measure (few-shot accuracy versus token-loss difference), model scale, and whether ablations exclude heads scoring highly for the other mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: Many eventual FV heads have high induction scores early in training; these decline as FV scores rise. The reverse is never observed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction heads serve as developmental precursors of function-vector heads.

fits_no_version.finding: FV scores emerge around step 16,000, much later than induction heads, and rise gradually through the end of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FV heads form later and more gradually than induction heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Top induction and FV heads overlap little (0–15%), but each sits around the 90–95th percentile on the other score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction and FV heads are distinct but correlated.

record.problems: The supplied text presents many results as plots without exact numerical values. Training-dynamics analysis is limited to Pythia checkpoints; the study does not vary training data or setup. The token-loss and task-accuracy measures lead to different conclusions, and the study does not test the proposed circuit composition directly.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model ablation curves and per-task accuracy curves are shown in Figures 8–9 and 15–18, but the supplied text does not give their exact values and the results are summarized in the retained aggregate rows. Other plotted results on head locations, score distributions, and ablation-overlap percentages are not direct tests of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no previous-token-head composition analysis and no small attention-only models; the induction score is only a prefix-matching attention measure.
The loss-curve bump, and the ICL gain measured by token-loss difference over training.
Whether induction heads carry 'most' token-loss ICL in absolute terms. Effects are compared with FV and random ablation, not with total ICL.
Other architectures and modalities, and multiple training seeds.
All of it. Training data and setup are not varied.
Which other mechanisms beyond FV heads carry few-shot learning.
All of it. Sub-steps of induction-head formation are not analysed.

missing.what: In the smallest model (Pythia 70M), induction and FV heads have similar causal effects on few-shot ICL accuracy.
The few-shot ablation results hold under random-head-replacement and zero ablation, not only mean ablation.
Per-model few-shot and token-loss ablation curves for all 12 models, including GPT-2 and Llama 2.

record.verdict_notes: V3 is scored only on token-loss-difference rows, because V3 defines ICL as loss falling with token index; the few-shot accuracy rows go to V6. V1 is not tested: the induction score is attention-only, and no attention-only small models are trained. Result values come from plots; the text gives no numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Measures induction scores on repeated-token sequences, but does not test composition with an earlier previous-token head or test the proposed circuit in small attention-only transformers.
Tracks induction scores and few-shot accuracy during training, but does not report a training-loss bump or test the specified token-loss event.
Tests few-shot accuracy and token-loss difference under ablation, but does not establish what carries most ICL in all large transformers or measure loss falling by token index in the original setup.
Studies 12 decoder-only models from Pythia, GPT-2, and Llama 2 families, but not other architectures, modalities, or a broad range of independent training runs.
Does not vary training data or setup to test their effects on induction-head formation or persistence of ICL.
Tests head ablations on few-shot task accuracy, but does not identify all other heads or mechanisms that may contribute to few-shot learning.
Does not test whether induction-head formation itself consists of multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
